content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin seeds are the edible kernels of the pumpkin (Cucurbita pepo). They have a mild nutty flavor, a crunchy texture, and are often eaten raw or lightly roasted. Unsalted seeds are suitable for diet-conscious eating and are used in cooking, baking, and as a topping for dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin seeds have long been a staple in North American and Eastern European cuisines.
They are a good source of zinc, an essential mineral for immune function.
In ancient cultures, pumpkins and their seeds symbolized abundance and protection from evil spirits.
Pumpkin seeds are commonly used as bird feed and for small livestock.
Seeds can be green or yellow depending on the pumpkin variety.

items.title: Rich in zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune health, wound healing, and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Seeds provide essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin E and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Polyunsaturated fatty acids help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pumpkin seeds.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite their benefits, seeds are calorie‑dense and should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or roasting can mitigate this.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pumpkin seeds can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, yogurt, oatmeal, baked goods, or blended into a seed butter. They also make a crunchy topping for soups and stews. Soaking the seeds for a few hours and then drying them yields a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil oxidation. Discard any seeds that develop a rancid smell.
